analysis.one_liner: Taxes investment gains at the same income tax rates as wages.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with no cosponsors in the final weeks of the 113th Congress and died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Rep. Alan Grayson's bill would repeal the part of the tax code that caps the tax rate on capital gains — the profits from selling stocks, real estate, and other investments — currently taxed at a maximum of 20% for long-term gains. Instead, all investment income would be taxed at the same top rates as regular wages, up to 39.6%. Because investment income is concentrated among the wealthiest households, the change would raise the most revenue from the top of the income scale.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers whose wages are taxed at full rates, since investment income would no longer get a lower rate; and public services, if the added revenue (which independent analysts have generally estimated in the tens to hundreds of billions annually for such proposals) were kept rather than returned elsewhere.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the "Maximum capital gains rate" provision in section 1(h) of the Internal Revenue Code, ending the lower preferential rates for capital gains income [S3].
Per the CRS summary, the bill amends the Internal Revenue Code to repeal the provisions allowing a lower income tax rate for capital gains income [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Wealthy households with large stock and asset holdings, whose gains would jump from a maximum 20% federal rate to the top ordinary rates of up to 39.6% — plus higher earners overall, since upper-income taxpayers hold most capital gains.

drawbacks.text: Critics of taxing capital gains as ordinary income argue it discourages investment, saving, and risk-taking; defenders of the lower rate say some benefit to investors ultimately flows to retirement accounts and business formation.

The bill as written applies to all capital gains income without carve-outs for middle-class savers, home sellers, or small business owners, so a hostile reader would call it blunt; the CRS summary and bill text show no such exemptions [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core trade-off is straightforward: most of the new burden falls on the wealthiest households, who own the large majority of taxable capital gains, while the added revenue could offset taxes on wages or fund services. The serious objections are economic — that higher tax on investment returns reduces saving, investment, and entrepreneurial risk-taking — and design: the one-page bill imposes the change with no exemptions or transition rules, which even supporters of the principle might want to modify.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and stayed there until the Congress ended, with no hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Alan Grayson introduced the Dollar is a Dollar Act on December 11, 2014, with the stated purpose of taxing capital gains at the same rate as ordinary income [S1][S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction, and no further action was recorded for the remainder of the 113th Congress [S5].
With 0 cosponsors and no committee action beyond the initial referral, the bill never advanced to a hearing or a vote before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households with large capital gains — the group the bill would have taxed at higher rates — are better off because the bill died in committee without ever reaching a vote; the preferential 20% capital gains rate remains in place.

for.name: Rep. Alan Grayson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 11, 2014, in the final weeks of the 113th Congress [S1].

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Dave Camp (R-MI)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after its December 11, 2014 referral; no hearing, markup, or report was scheduled before the Congress ended [S5].

against.name: House colleagues
against.what_they_did: None signed on as cosponsors; the bill ended the Congress with zero [S4].

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor is a Democrat and it drew no cosponsors of either party; with no votes recorded, the partisan split can only be inferred from its isolated, party-left sponsorship.

industries.note: The bill would eliminate the 20% maximum rate on long-term capital gains and tax investment profits at ordinary income rates up to 39.6%, a direct cost concentrated at the top of the wealth distribution. The outcome left the preferential rate untouched.

Higher taxes on realized gains can discourage frequent trading and sales of appreciated assets, reducing activity that generates fees for brokers, fund managers, and advisors. The bill died, so no change occurred.

industries.industry: Venture capital and small business finance
industries.note: A core argument for the preferential rate is that it rewards risk-taking in startups and small business investment; taxing gains as ordinary income would raise the tax cost of successful exits. The bill contained no carve-outs to protect these investors [S3].
